source.title: Principled Weight Initialization for Hypernetworks
source.authors: Oscar Chang; Lampros Flokas; H. Lipson

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text contains the full paper and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: Compares initialization methods and reports their effects on training loss and convergence in hypernetworks, a different setting from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own initialization comparisons and training outcomes. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as rows. Several outcomes are described in text while their plotted values are figure-only; no training classification error is reported.
record.test_reason: The study uses variance-preserving initialization principles to develop and evaluate hypernetwork initialization. Its optimization results concern training hypernetworks that generate another network's weights, whereas V4 concerns initialization and training of plain networks. The classical-network comparator and appendix comparison of initialization means do not isolate V4's claimed effects. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that hyperfan produces appropriately scaled generated weights, improves stability and convergence, and enables SGD training in every tested experiment. They find no consistent reason to prefer hyperfan-in over hyperfan-out.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares newly derived hypernetwork initialization methods with classical and heuristic hypernetwork initializations; its experiments train hypernetworks that generate mainnet weights.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization choice changes training outcomes. For CIFAR-10, Kaiming fan-in did not train, fan-out began around epoch 270, and both hyperfan methods trained immediately. On ImageNet, Kaiming fan-out performed similarly to hyperfan methods, while fan-in had higher initial loss and slower training.

fits_no_version.finding: Hyperfan improves stability and convergence in hypernetwork training. On CIFAR-10, Kaiming fan-in fails, fan-out starts learning around epoch 270, and both hyperfan variants train immediately. On ImageNet, fan-in trains more slowly while fan-out performs similarly to hyperfan.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scaled for generated mainnet weights can improve hypernetwork optimization; its advantage over classical initialization depends on the initialization variant and setting.

fits_no_version.finding: In continual regression learning, hyperfan yields lower initial, intermediate, and final training losses across three tasks, averaged over 15 runs. Kaiming fan-in trains only at the smallest tested learning rate, 0.00001.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hypernetwork initialization affects attainable training loss and usable learning rates in continual regression learning.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix B.1.3 reports no significant benefit from harmonic, geometric, or arithmetic combinations of fan-in and fan-out formulas in either classical networks or hypernetworks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combining forward- and backward-derived initialization variances does not necessarily improve training over either formula alone.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 discussion reports training success and delay but no numerical training-loss values in text. MNIST and ImageNet loss comparisons are shown in plots without transcribed values. The experiments concern hypernetworks and do not report training classification error.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in directly trained large convolutional networks, corrupted or random labels, and model-size or regularization qualifications.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious minima, and the effect of extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization exceptions.
Initialization effects on learning speed and trainable depth in plain networks, including orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization and very deep convolutional networks.
Recovery above an initial stability threshold, curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability training, and divergence relative to that threshold.
Training-speed and learning-rate comparisons with versus without batch normalization, and the Fixup exception.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the supplied claim versions because all rows map to none; this does not negate the explicitly reported hypernetwork outcomes. The record incorrectly says no results were omitted: continual-learning results and the appendix initialization-mean comparison are absent, but neither warrants a missing entry for these versions.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training classification error, random or corrupted labels, or the stated model-size and early-stopping comparisons.
Does not test two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks, spurious local minima, or student width relative to teacher width.
Does not compare plain and residual networks or test depth, shortcuts, or normalization as described.
Tests hypernetwork initialization methods, not the stated initialization comparisons and trainable-depth claims for plain networks.
Does not test learning rates above a stability limit or measure sharpness and the catapult or edge-of-stability behavior.
Does not compare batch normalization with no normalization for training speed or learning-rate tolerance as stated.

rows.subject: classical network with Xavier init
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST for 30 epochs with Xavier initialization.
rows.note: Included as a comparator in the reported MNIST loss plot; plotted values are not transcribed in the text.
rows.check: A classical Xavier-initialized network is a comparator, without an alternative classical initialization establishing V4's effect. Its learning rate is 0.01 versus 0.0005 for the hypernetworks; this matters when comparing convergence.

rows.check: Training hypernetwork parameters does not test V4's plain-network claim. The text establishes exploding initial activations and unstable generated weights, but numerical training-loss values cannot be recovered from the supplied plot text.
